items.title: Expired pastes vanish only when the file is next saved
items.body:
**Key: on the next save of pastes.json, which filters out expired pastes before writing.**

`WriteAllUnsafeAsync` does not write the list it is given as-is. It first keeps only `!p.IsExpired(...)` entries, then writes those. So any save (a create, an update, a delete, or even a read that bumps a view count) also drops every expired paste from the file. Nothing else removes them.

Why the others are wrong:
- *The first read deletes it*: when `GetAsync` sees an expired paste it returns `null` straight away, without writing anything.
- *A background timer*: there is no scheduler or hosted worker in the repo.
- *Stays on disk forever*: it stays only until the next save of any kind.

excerpts.quote: if (paste is null || paste.IsExpired(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow)) { return null; }

items.title: A one-letter search is refused twice over
items.body:
**Key: 400 ProblemDetails; without it, the store's own check still returns 200 [].**

The search route checks first: if `q` is blank or shorter than 2 characters after trimming, it returns `Results.BadRequest` with "Search query must be at least 2 characters." So `q=a` gets 400.

If you deleted that route check, `SearchPublicAsync` would still trim the query and `return []` when it is shorter than 2, before it takes the lock or reads the file. The route would then answer 200 with an empty list. Having the same rule in two layers is called defence in depth.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Without it, each call scans every paste*: the store's early `return []` stops before any reading. The full scan only happens for queries of 2+ characters (the risk register's "Search full scan").
- *200 with the 20 newest*: the route refuses the query first.
- *404*: `/api/pastes/search` is its own route, not a slug lookup.

excerpts.quote: if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(q) || q.Trim().Length < 2) { return Results.BadRequest(new ProblemDetails("Search query must be at least 2 characters.")); }

items.title: How the store reads and writes one JSON file
items.body:
There is no database. `PasteStore` keeps every paste in one file, `App_Data/pastes.json`. Every operation follows the same pattern, often called read-modify-write:

1. Wait for the store's lock (`_gate`).
2. Read and deserialize the whole file into a list (`ReadAllUnsafeAsync`).
3. Find or change entries in that list.
4. If something changed, serialize the whole list back to the file (`WriteAllUnsafeAsync`).
5. Release the lock in a `finally` block.

The word "Unsafe" in the helper names means "call this only while holding the lock". The persistence guide's table summarizes it: whole-file read, whole-file rewrite, and a lock that is process-local.

While you read, look closely at what `WriteAllUnsafeAsync` does to the list before it writes. It is not a plain dump of the list it receives.

readMore.why: What a move to EF Core would involve, and how to add a field without breaking old JSON.

items.title: A wrong delete key answers 404, like a missing paste
items.body:
**Key: 404 with one blended message, same as a missing or expired paste.**

The PUT route first runs `request.Validate()`. The body is well formed, so there are no errors and no 400. Then `UpdateAsync` returns `null` in three cases with one `if`: no paste, expired paste, or a key hash that does not match. The route cannot tell which case happened and maps every `null` to `Results.NotFound` with "Paste not found, expired, or delete key is incorrect." The auth guide lists this under senior checks: auth errors are not distinguishable.

Why the others are wrong:
- *400 from Validate()*: `Validate` checks the shape of the body (content length, key length), not whether the key matches a stored paste.
- *401 Unauthorized*: no route returns 401, and there is no authentication in the app.
- *403 with a field error*: no route returns 403; field errors come only from `Validate`.

excerpts.quote: var paste = await store.UpdateAsync(slug, request); if (paste is null) { return Results.NotFound(new ProblemDetails("Paste not found, expired, or delete key is incorrect.")); }
if (paste is null || paste.IsExpired(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow) || paste.DeleteKeyHash != HashDeleteKey(request.DeleteKey))
Are auth errors distinguishable? Wrong key and missing paste both return not found

items.title: Reading a paste also rewrites the whole file
items.body:
**Key: bumps ViewCount and LastViewedAt, then rewrites the whole pastes.json file.**

After finding a live paste, `GetAsync` builds a copy with `ViewCount + 1` and `LastViewedAt` set to now (`with` creates a modified copy of a record). It puts the copy back into the list and calls `WriteAllUnsafeAsync(pastes)`, which serializes the entire list to disk. So every successful GET is also a write. The key-flows guide uses this as a lesson in command/query separation: "Reads mutate disk."

Why the others are wrong:
- *Appends to a separate analytics log*: there is no other log file; the paste record itself changes.
- *In memory, saved later*: the write happens inside `GetAsync`, before it returns.
- *No side effects*: lines 36-44 change and save the record.

excerpts.quote: var updated = paste with { ViewCount = paste.ViewCount + 1, LastViewedAt = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow };
A read has a side effect: it increments view count. This is a useful lesson in command/query separation.

items.title: One SemaphoreSlim guards the file, inside one process only
items.body:
**Key: one SemaphoreSlim(1,1) serializes store operations, but only within one process.**

`new SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)` is a lock that lets one caller in at a time. Every public store method starts with `await _gate.WaitAsync()` and releases it in `finally`, so the two creates run one after the other: the second reads the file only after the first has written it. The store is registered as a singleton, so all requests share the same `_gate`.

The limit: the semaphore lives in this process's memory. A second copy of the server would have its own semaphore and could still overwrite the first one's writes. The risk register lists this as "Process-local lock only".

Why the others are wrong:
- *No protection*: the gate is there and used by every method.
- *An OS file lock from File.OpenRead*: the stream is opened and closed inside the read helper; it does not cover the whole read-modify-write.
- *Optimistic retries*: no code compares `UpdatedAt` or retries.

excerpts.quote: | Process-local lock only | [PasteStore.cs](../../../backend/Data/PasteStore.cs#L14-L14) | Race under multi-instance |

items.title: ResolveExpiry: Never means null, unknown falls back to a day
items.body:
**Key: Never gives a null ExpiresAt; the fallback arm quietly assigns one day.**

`ResolveExpiry` is a C# `switch` expression. Each arm maps one enum value to an expiry time. `PasteExpiration.Never => null` means "no expiry date". The last arm, `_ => now.AddDays(1)`, is the discard pattern: it matches anything not listed above, so an unknown value silently gets one day. In practice an unknown value rarely gets here, because `CreatePasteRequest.Validate` checks `Enum.IsDefined(Expiration)` first.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Never gives MaxValue; unknown throws*: the arm says `null`, and no arm throws.
- *Both reach the default arm*: `Never` has its own arm above the `_` arm, and the first matching arm wins.
- *Never is rejected in validation*: `Never` is a defined enum value, so `Enum.IsDefined` accepts it.

items.title: Start here: a pastebin with one store class and one JSON file
items.body:
This pack is about a small Pastebin clone: an ASP.NET Core Minimal API backend and a React page. Almost every quiz is answered by two files, `backend/Program.cs` (the HTTP routes) and `backend/Data/PasteStore.cs` (all reading and writing of `pastes.json`). The upskill docs explain what those files do and what is risky about them.

Suggested reading order:

1. `docs/upskill/README.md`: what the app is and what it deliberately lacks (no tests, no database, no auth framework).
2. `docs/upskill/01-codebase-cartography/05-key-flows.md`: each user action (create, read, edit, search, delete) traced step by step.
3. `backend/Program.cs` lines 31-113: every route and the status code it returns.
4. `backend/Data/PasteStore.cs`: read it top to bottom; it is 250 lines.
5. `docs/upskill/03-architecture-and-patterns/02-data-model-and-persistence.md` and `03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md`.
6. `docs/upskill/08-reference/risk-register.md`: the known risks in one table.

For each store method, write down: what it checks, what it changes, and when it saves the file.

excerpts.quote: There is no test project, CI workflow, EF Core DbContext, auth framework, Docker setup, or hosted worker in this repo as inspected; those appear in this lab as explicit gaps and design exercises.

readMore.why: Junior, mid-level and senior reading paths through the code, each with what to read a file for.
The weekend path if you want a quick map before the drills.

items.title: Permissions without accounts: the delete key
items.body:
The app has no users and no login. Anyone with a paste's link (its slug) can read it. To edit or delete a paste you must also know its delete key, a secret the creator typed when making it. The guide gives the precise name: authorization by possession of a shared secret, not authentication. In other words, the app checks that you know the secret; it never learns who you are.

This model has typical weak spots, and the guide lists the questions a senior reviewer asks: is the secret ever logged or put in a URL, can someone try many guesses, and can an attacker tell different failures apart from the error messages?

Before the quizzes, read how the store turns the key into what it saves (`HashDeleteKey`) and compare the guard `if` lines at the top of `UpdateAsync` and `DeleteAsync` clause by clause.

excerpts.quote: Precise term: this is authorization by possession of a shared secret, not authentication. It does not identify a user.
- Treating a random slug as permission. - Trusting hidden UI controls.

readMore.why: A short threat-model drill for delete: what stops a key-guessing attacker today, and what you would add.

items.title: The slug alphabet leaves out look-alike characters
items.body:
**Key: l, I, O, 0 and 1, the look-alikes that people easily misread.**

Read the alphabet string slowly. Lowercase runs `abcdefghijk` then `mnop...`: there is no `l` (25 letters). Uppercase runs `ABCDEFGH` then `JKLMN` then `PQR...`: no `I` and no `O` (24 letters). Digits are `23456789`: no `0` and no `1` (8 digits). 25 + 24 + 8 = 57. These five are the characters people confuse when reading or typing a link (l/I/1, O/0).

Why the others are wrong:
- *Hyphen and underscore*: they were never in the string, and nothing suggests they would break routing; the string simply has letters and digits only.
- *The vowels*: `a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, `u` and `A`, `E`, `U` are all present.
- *Uppercase letters*: most uppercase letters are present.

items.title: Case-insensitive slugs: two spellings, one paste
items.body:
**Key: abC234xy and ABc234XY name the same paste, shrinking the effective namespace.**

`SlugEquals` compares with `OrdinalIgnoreCase`, so it treats upper and lower case as the same. Every lookup (get, update, delete) uses it, and so does the collision loop in `CreateUniqueSlugAsync`, which keeps drawing a new slug while any existing one is "equal". So two slugs that differ only in case point to the same paste, and the mixed-case alphabet does not give as many distinct addresses as it seems to.

Why the others are wrong:
- *Lookups case-sensitive, creation not*: both use the same ignore-case comparison, so no duplicates are minted.
- *Lookups unaffected*: `GetAsync`, `UpdateAsync` and `DeleteAsync` all find the paste through `SlugEquals`.
- *Lowercased before saving*: `CreateAsync` stores the slug exactly as `RandomToken` made it; nothing lowercases it.

excerpts.quote: private static bool SlugEquals(string left, string right) => string.Equals(left, right, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);

items.title: Only DELETE still works on an expired, unpurged paste
items.body:
**Key: DELETE alone: its guard checks existence and the key hash, not expiry.**

Put the two guards side by side.

- `UpdateAsync`: `paste is null || paste.IsExpired(...) || paste.DeleteKeyHash != ...`
- `DeleteAsync`: `paste is null || paste.DeleteKeyHash != ...`

The update guard has an expiry clause, so an expired paste returns `null` and the route answers 404. The delete guard has no expiry clause: the paste is still in the list (it has not been purged yet), the key matches, so it is removed and the method returns `true`.

Why the others are wrong:
- *PUT alone, update renews expiry*: `UpdateAsync` refuses expired pastes, and it does not touch `ExpiresAt`.
- *Both*: the update guard does check `IsExpired`.
- *Neither*: `DeleteAsync` never calls `IsExpired`.

excerpts.quote: if (paste is null || paste.IsExpired(DateTimeOffset.UtcNow) || paste.DeleteKeyHash != HashDeleteKey(request.DeleteKey))
if (paste is null || paste.DeleteKeyHash != HashDeleteKey(deleteKey)) { return false; }

items.title: The delete key is stored as an unsalted SHA-256 hex hash
items.body:
**Key: as an unsalted, hex-encoded SHA-256 hash of the key.**

`HashDeleteKey` turns the key into UTF-8 bytes, runs `SHA256.HashData` on them and stores `Convert.ToHexString(bytes)`. `CreateAsync` saves that string as `DeleteKeyHash`, so the raw key never lands in `pastes.json`. Later, update and delete hash the key the caller sends and compare the two strings.

"Unsalted" means the same key always gives the same hash, and SHA-256 is fast, so this protects against someone simply reading the file, but it is not a slow password hash. The architecture critique calls it "safe-ish".

Why the others are wrong:
- *bcrypt with a salt*: there is no bcrypt in the code and no package references at all.
- *Plaintext*: the store only ever saves the hash.
- *Kept in memory*: there is no in-memory key table; the hash is in the JSON record.

excerpts.quote: | Safe-ish secret persistence | [HashDeleteKey](../../../backend/Data/PasteStore.cs#L236-L240) | Avoids raw delete-key storage. |
